Efficacy and safety of QY201, an oral dual Janus kinase 1/tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor, in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 dose-finding trial.
abstract: QY201 is a novel oral Janus kinase 1 and tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor. To evaluate the efficacy of multiple QY201 doses in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (AD), and to inform dose selection for phase 3 studies. In this phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 200 adults with moderate-to-severe AD were randomized 1:1:1:1 to receive QY201 (5 mg, 10 mg, or 20 mg twice daily [BID]) or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving ≥75% improvement in Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-75) at week 12. EASI-75 response rates at week 12 were 72.9%, 84.7% and 81.4% in the 5 mg BID, 10 mg BID, and 20 mg BID groups, respectively, compared with 18.5% in the placebo group (all P<0.0001). Investigator's Global Assessment response rates were 44.7% (P=0.0011), 64.3% (P<0.0001), and 71.3% (P<0.0001), respectively, versus 12.4% with placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 74.0%, 75.5%, and 90.4% of patients receiving QY201, compared to 69.4% with placebo; most were mild or moderate. Short follow-up and single-country population. The phase 2 findings support further evaluation of QY201 at doses of 10 mg BID and 20 mg BID in confirmatory phase 3 trials.

Joint American Academy of Dermatology-Hidradenitis Suppurativa Foundation guidelines of care for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa.
abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa affects 0.7% to 1.5% of the global population and causes substantial disability and meaningfully impairs quality of life. To provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa. A workgroup conducted a systematic review and applied the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach to assess the certainty of evidence and to develop recommendations. This guideline presents 37 evidence-based recommendations. Strong recommendations are made for adalimumab, bimekizumab, infliximab, secukinumab, and routine pain assessment. Conditional recommendations are made for topical clindamycin, resorcinol, and ruxolitinib; oral doxycycline, tetracycline, and clindamycin with rifampin; intravenous ertapenem; spironolactone; short-term systemic corticosteroids; upadacitinib; specific procedural interventions; tobacco cessation; supportive pain management; and zinc supplementation and vitamin D repletion. Analysis is limited to best evidence available from systematic review. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa.

title: The pyrin inflammasome senses OCTN2-mediated uptake of extracellular ʟ-carnitine from muscle injury or ingestion.
abstract: Red-meat-containing diets are epidemiologically associated with diseases of chronic inflammation, while diets that restrict red meat improve health. Yet, it is uncertain how red meat incites inflammation. Here, we discover that ʟ-carnitine, an amino acid highly concentrated in skeletal muscle myocytes, drives inflammasome activation in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-challenged mice and LPS-primed murine and human macrophages. We find that extracellular ʟ-carnitine represses mevalonate synthesis, thereby triggering activation of the pyrin inflammasome, downstream of cellular import by the high-affinity ʟ-carnitine transporter OCTN2. We find that the inflammatory response to skeletal muscle injury also requires pyrin and OCTN2. Thus, in summary, we identify macrophages as sentinels of exogenous and endogenous extracellular ʟ-carnitine that serve as a proxy for skeletal myocyte damage, and we open the field to examine the mechanistic basis for how excess dietary intake of carnitine-rich food drives inflammatory disease.

title: A microbiome-bile acid axis mediates protection from chronic liver disease in females.
abstract: Sex-based differences in chronic liver disease (CLD) incidence and progression are well documented, yet the mechanistic basis of this sexual disparity remains elusive. Here, leveraging a large-scale metabolomics database comprising 9,254 individuals, we identify the endogenous bile acid, isoursodeoxycholic acid (isoUDCA), as a candidate mediator of female-associated hepatoprotection. We trace the origin of isoUDCA to a bacterial consortium, which is selectively enriched by estrogen through shaping a specialized intestinal microenvironment. Mechanistically, isoUDCA promotes the nuclear accumulation of SREBP2. This upregulates the intracellular transporter STARD4 and its functionally coupled downstream enzyme CYP7B1, thereby facilitating intracellular cholesterol handling and metabolic conversion. Collectively, our findings support a microbiome-bile acid-liver axis that may contribute to sex differences in CLD susceptibility and support further evaluation of isoUDCA as a potential therapeutic intervention.

title: CD300f acts as an inducible inhibitory checkpoint that limits mast cell activation by suppressing MITF-dependent activation.
abstract: Mast cells (MCs) are key regulators of cutaneous immune responses and play a central role in allergic and non-IgE-mediated skin inflammation by activating the Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2). The inhibitory receptor CD300f has been shown to modulate MC activation, but its role in regulating MRGPRX2-dependent signaling remains unclear. Here, we investigated CD300f expression and function in human skin MCs and its impact on MRGPRX2-mediated responses, with some comparison to IgE-mediated responses. CD300f was expressed on human skin MCs, and its surface expression increased following MRGPRX2 activation. Engagement of CD300f significantly attenuated MC activation induced by MRGPRX2-dependent stimuli, including substance P, vancomycin, and quinolone drugs. Transcriptomic analyses in CD300f-LAD2 revealed that CD300f signaling suppressed activation-associated gene programs after substance P stimulation, including NF-κB and MAPK pathways. Notably, CD300f engagement markedly downregulated microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), as confirmed at the protein level in LAD2 and skin MCs. MITF inhibition with TT012 and CD300f triggering enhance inhibitory responses, decreasing MITF and MITF-target expression more strongly. Conversely, lysyl-tRNA synthetase overexpression increases MITF expression and significantly reduces CD300f-mediated inhibition of both MRGPRX2- and FcεRI-dependent signaling. These findings reveal a CD300f-MITF regulatory axis that limits skin MC activation and inflammatory responses.

Efficacy and safety of litifilimab in cutaneous lupus erythematosus: 24-week results of the randomized phase 2 study, AMETHYST.
abstract: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) is a serious autoimmune disease with no approved targeted treatments. Evaluate the efficacy and safety of litifilimab in AMETHYST Part A (Phase 2). AMETHYST is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase 2/3 study that investigates litifilimab in participants with CLE. Participants were randomized to receive litifilimab 225 mg or placebo every 4 weeks during Weeks 0-24. The primary endpoint was the Cutaneous Lupus Activity Investigator's Global Assessment-Revised (CLA-IGA-R) erythema score of 0-1 at Week 16, with several Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Disease Area and Severity Index (CLASI)-based endpoints at Week 24 as secondary endpoints. Safety was also assessed. Significantly more participants treated with litifilimab achieved clear/almost clear skin (CLA-IGA-R erythema 0-1) than those treated with placebo at Week 16 (14.7% vs 2.9%, P= .0263). Additionally, more participants treated with litifilimab achieved CLASI-70 response vs placebo at Week 24 (21.7% vs 5.8%, P = .0195). Litifilimab was generally well tolerated; safety data were consistent with prior studies. Study was not powered to detect statistically significant differences in secondary endpoints. Litifilimab treatment led to greater improvements in skin disease activity vs placebo and was well tolerated in participants with CLE through Week 24.

EGFR activity governs stage-dependent fibrotic responses in recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
abstract: Repeated injury can impair transitions between cellular phenotypes, potentially leading to pathological tissue repair. In recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB), collagen VII deficiency predisposes to repeated tissue injury, driving inflammation and fibrosis. Although fibroblasts are major effector cells in RDEB fibrosis, their phenotypic and molecular changes underlying disease progression remain elusive. Through cellular and in situ analyses of clinical samples and tissue from an RDEB mouse model, we disclose a phenotypic switch in dermal fibroblasts during disease progression. At early stages, fibroblasts display a contractile phenotype, whereas at later stages they transition toward a less contractile phenotype with increased production of a fibrosis-promoting extracellular matrix, indicated by high tenascin-C levels. Dysregulated epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling through AKT appears central to this switch. At early stages, EGFR signaling and AKT support fibroblast contractility, whereas at later stages this signaling becomes intrinsically blunted, with ADAM17 implicated in the transition. The type of inflammation modulates this phenotypic switch. Thus, RDEB fibroblasts transition from a contractile to a less contractile but pro-fibrotic phenotype during disease progression. These findings suggest that reducing cellular contractility may be advantageous at earlier disease stages, whereas extracellular matrix-targeting strategies may have higher priority at later stages.

title: Vitiligo-associated variants and genes beyond immune-related loci: A genome-wide association and Mendelian randomization meta-analysis.
abstract: Although past genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified over 50 susceptible loci associated with vitiligo risk, few have systematically explored causality among potentially associated variants and genes. To address this, we analyzed summary statistics from 3 large-scale genomic resources, including the Million Veteran Program, United Kingdom Biobank, and FinnGen. Cases were defined using ICD-9 code 709.01 or ICD-10 code L80, including all studies that contributed genome-wide summary statistics and limiting analyses to loci with ≥1 common variant (minor allele frequency ≥1%). METAL was used to conduct a fixed effects inverse variance-weighted meta-analysis with kinship adjustment. Variant-to-gene (V2G) mapping was performed using the Open Targets V2G framework. title: A phenome-wide structural variant map from 467,152 UK Biobank genomes.
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are large (>50 base pairs) genomic rearrangements that can significantly influence human phenotypes, yet their contribution to health and disease remains undercharacterized. We conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) of 1.6 million SVs identified in whole-genome sequencing data from 467,152 UK Biobank participants, across 13,322 binary, 2,018 quantitative, and 2,923 plasma protein traits. Of these, 82.25% of SVs were outside the detectable range of prior copy-number variant studies. Protein quantitative trait loci analysis linked 3,241 SVs to 1,608 proteins, with effects dependent on SV type and location. In SV-PheWAS, we detected 28,184 associations with human health outcomes. Notably, we uncovered rare SVs with strong phenotypic effects. Furthermore, we show that at known genome-wide association study loci, 32.21% of associated SVs overlapped functional genomic regions. This study underscores the underestimated role of SVs in human genetics and their potential to advance understanding of human biology and drug discovery.

title: Mitochondria-targeted tetraoxanes initiate lipid peroxidation to drive ferroptosis and tumor suppression.
abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated as a vulnerability in multiple cancers, yet approaches for effectively inducing ferroptosis in vivo are limited. Bypassing conventional strategies targeting the antiferroptotic glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) proteins, we designed metabolic initiators of lipid peroxidation (MILPOs) and developed the compounds WMK-1/2, which contain tetraoxane radical-generating and mitochondria-targeting groups, as de novo ferroptosis inducers. WMK-1 localizes primarily to mitochondria, induces local lipid peroxidation, and impairs oxidative phosphorylation. WMK-1 induces a "mito-ferroptosis" sub-pathway that skips GPX4 inhibition as a prerequisite, can be rescued by lipophilic radical-trapping antioxidants, yet is minimally sensitive to acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) perturbation and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation, and evades retinol-mediated protection. Instead, WMK-1-induced cell death requires labile Fe

title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise.
abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

title: An opioid efficacy switch for reversible optical control of analgesia.
abstract: The mu-opioid receptor (MOR) is a major target for pain treatment, but its effectiveness is limited by dangerous side effects. However, the systemic administration of opioids makes it difficult both to decipher their underlying mechanisms of action and to limit drug action to specific receptor subpopulations to isolate therapeutic effects from adverse effects. Here, we develop a reversibly photoswitchable morphinan agonist termed "azo-morphine-3" (AM-3) that interconverts from low to high efficacy in response to light to enable optical control of MOR signaling. Structural analysis of the low ("trans") and high ("cis") efficacy states of AM-3 bound to the MOR reveals distinct binding modes, with each state driving unique ligand, receptor, and G protein dynamics. In mice, AM-3 drives reversible and repeatable optical control of antinociception across pain models with a reduced side effect profile owing to its limited brain accumulation and its ability to be locally activated.

title: Functional diversification of the cephalopod proteome by RNA editing.
abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.

title: Cellular self-organization orchestrates ferroptosis propagation.
abstract: Self-organization generates cellular patterns that guide morphogenesis, but how it regulates collective cell fate remains underexplored. We show that cellular self-organization constrains the propagation of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of oxidative cell death that can otherwise spread as unbounded trigger waves. The spatial patterning of cell density and alignment encodes transcriptional programs, priming cells toward ferroptosis-sensitive or -resistant fates. Low-density, misaligned regions with elevated YAP/TEAD1 activity are sensitive, whereas high-density, aligned regions with increased NRF2 expression form propagation-resistant boundaries. Cell elongation establishes a polarized distribution of oxidizable lipids, creating peroxidation hotspots at the cell poles that promote propagation along cell alignment. In silico and pharmacological perturbations reveal that pattern-dependent susceptibility and polarized lipid organization act together to constrain isotropic waves into spatially confined, anisotropic propagation. These findings identify self-organization as a systems-level mechanism governing collective homeostasis, providing a paradigm to explore how tissue-scale organization regulates cell death in development and disease.

title: Spatiotemporal co-transcriptomics uncovers coordinated rhizobia-legume stress programs supporting nitrogen fixation in Medicago.
abstract: Rhizobial nitrogen fixation in legume nodules requires precise spatial and temporal coordination between host and bacterial gene expression. Here, we applied spatial enhanced resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) to profile Medicago nodules across five developmental stages, generating a co-transcriptomic atlas of nodule development. Using a mixed-probe capture strategy, we simultaneously detected host and rhizobial transcripts within the same tissue sections, enabling analysis of host-microbe transcriptional coordination during symbiosis. We identified dynamic changes in host cell composition and developmental trajectories and uncovered two transcription factors, MtERF82 and MtDOF53, required for maintenance of the indeterminate nodule meristem. Rhizobial and host genes exhibited stage- and zone-specific expression patterns along the nodule apex-to-base axis. Notably, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated stress responses in both host cells and rhizobia were linked to symbiotic nitrogen fixation. Functional analyses further showed that MtERF71 and MtCBF1 promote nitrogen fixation by regulating ROS homeostasis and activating key symbiotic genes, highlighting stress signaling as an integral component of mutualistic symbiosis.

title: A telomere-to-telomere map of somatic mutation burden and functional impact in a cancer.
abstract: Cancer genomes harbor extensive somatic genetic and epigenetic variation, yet large portions of the genome remain inaccessible to conventional reference-based analyses. Here, we demonstrate that pairing a near-telomere-to-telomere (near-T2T) diploid assembly of a donor with deep short- and long-read sequencing of their melanoma reveals that 16% of somatic variants localize to sequences absent from GRCh38, with satellite repeats acting as hotspots for UV-associated mutagenesis. Centromere kinetochore binding domains emerge as focal sites of chromosome arm aneuploidy breakpoints and somatic genetic variation, features we further demonstrate are also present in non-cancerous tissues. By contrast, extensive epigenetic remodeling of kinetochore binding domains appears specific to oncogenesis. Single-molecule telomere analyses reconstruct the cycle of telomere erosion and telomerase-mediated extension during tumor evolution, while haplotype-resolved chromatin maps reveal widespread somatic epimutations impacting regulatory elements. Together, these findings define previously inaccessible dimensions of somatic variation and establish a framework for telomere-to-telomere studies of human mosaicism.

title: Somatic epimutations cap genetic determinism in the human diploid chromatin epigenome.
abstract: Diploid human cells contain two non-identical genomes, and differences in their regulation underlie human development and disease. We present Fiber-seq inferred regulatory elements (FIRE) and show that FIRE provides a more comprehensive and quantitative snapshot of the accessible chromatin landscape across the 6 Gbp diploid human genome, overcoming previously unrecognized biases in existing regulatory element catalogs. FIRE enables comprehensive detection of haplotype-selective chromatin accessibility (HSCA), exposing imprinted elements lacking underlying parent-of-origin differences in DNA methylation and gene regulatory modules that permit genes to escape X chromosome inactivation. We uncover that the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus harbors the most HSCA in immune cells, where we resolve specific transcription factor (TF) binding events disrupted by disease-associated variants. Finally, we demonstrate that the regulatory landscape of a cell is littered with autosomal somatic chromatin epimutations that are propagated by clonal expansions to create mitotically stable and non-genetically deterministic chromatin alterations.

title: Comprehensive benchmarking of somatic mutation detection by the SMaHT Network.
abstract: Somatic mosaicism is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of human biology, yet the detection of somatic mutations remains challenging. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network conducted large-scale benchmarking experiments involving cell lines and donor tissues to evaluate sequencing technologies, experimental approaches, and computational methods for detecting different types of somatic mutations, generating community resources with >1,000× short-read and 100-400× long-read data for nine analyzed samples. We determined effective strategies for utilizing short- and long-read sequencing for mutation detection and demonstrated that using donor-specific and pangenome-inferred diploid assemblies improved calling, extending mutation catalogs to challenging genomic regions. We benchmarked six duplex technologies and showed that single-cell sequencing resolves cell-type-specific mutational patterns and heterogeneity. Our results indicate that bulk, single-cell, and duplex analyses are complementary and that leveraging all three provides comprehensive characterization of mosaicism within tissues. Together, these findings provide the scientific and clinical communities with a roadmap for accurate genome-wide somatic mutation analysis.

title: Charting the silent variation within us.
abstract: Every cell in the human body carries its own genome, shaped by mutations acquired over a lifetime, yet this vast somatic variation has been nearly impossible to measure. The SMaHT Network now delivers benchmarked tools and the first body-wide map of somatic mosaicism, establishing a baseline of "normal" against which its roles in development, aging, and disease can finally be tested.

title: Cellular scaling laws in the mammalian brain.
abstract: Recent whole-brain cell atlases have uncovered a consistent cytoarchitectural feature: the greatest diversity of discrete neuronal cell types resides not in the regions with the most neurons (e.g., the cortex and cerebellum) but rather in deep subcortical structures like the hypothalamus and brain stem. We propose that this discrepancy reflects a fundamental algorithmic division in the vertebrate brain between a "learning subsystem" and a "steering subsystem." The learning subsystem (cortex, striatum, and cerebellum) scales via the replication of repetitive modules to maximize computational capacity, analogous to scaling up parameters in machine learning models. By contrast, the steering subsystem (hypothalamus, pallidum, and brainstem) scales via diversification of bespoke cell types to encode innate drives and reflexes, functioning as a high-dimensional biological "reward function." This framework explains the divergence in how evolution has influenced these subsystems and offers a unified lens for understanding brain architecture and the etiology of brain disease; furthermore, it may inform model designs for artificial intelligence.

title: Milking the niche: Microbial control of neonatal hematopoiesis.
abstract: In this issue of Cell, Howard et al. reveal how the milk glycoprotein osteopontin shapes the neonatal microbiome to regulate hematopoiesis, promoting dendritic cell development and protection from severe respiratory infection. These findings uncover a maternal milk-microbiota pathway linking early-life nutrition to immune development and long-term disease susceptibility.

title: Immunoregulatory gene GIMAP6 suppresses lethal atherosclerotic vasculopathy and ischemic heart failure.
abstract: Controlling hyperlipidemia has reduced but not eliminated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) as a major cause of human mortality. Here, we report that loss of the immunoregulatory gene GTPase of immunity-associated protein 6 (Gimap6) in mice causes an inflammatory vasculopathy and accelerated atherosclerosis in the absence of hyperlipidemia. These vascular abnormalities cause progressive cardiac ischemia, myocardial infarction, and heart failure, culminating in early death. GIMAP6 loss precipitates early endothelial barrier failure and a mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS)-PPARγ-CD36 lipid-influx cascade that lowers the threshold for foam-cell formation and induces IL-6/MCP-1/TNF-mediated inflammation. Human hypomorphic GIMAP6 variants, including the African-ancestry-enriched V65I allele, are associated with altered monocyte redox balance, increased CD36-mediated lipid uptake, and early ASCVD. Thus, GIMAP6 is a crucial safeguard for vascular integrity that restrains endothelial dysfunction, macrophage foam cell generation, and inflammation that can cause lethal ASCVD independently of systemic hyperlipidemia.

title: Arabidopsis uses distinct coumarins and bacterial pathways for pH-adaptive iron acquisition.
abstract: Iron (Fe) limitation restricts plant growth in diverse soils, and root-associated microbes can alleviate plant Fe starvation. Whether plants integrate the edaphic environment and microbial activities into their Fe uptake strategies remains unclear. We show that bacterium-mediated alleviation of Fe deficiency in Arabidopsis functions at varying environmental pH and is taxonomically widespread among root microbiota isolates from soils with different edaphic profiles. This process is regulated by host-controlled and pH-adapted root exudation of different coumarin chemotypes. These exometabolites interact with root-associated bacteria to mobilize Fe either via bacterial siderophore-mediated chelation at circumneutral pH or redox-sensing-controlled, reduction-based pathways at acidic pH. The corresponding bacterial genes are prevalent in the root microbiota, and they likely evolved before the emergence of land plants. Our findings suggest that Fe malnutrition-induced exudation of redox-active metabolites by non-graminaceous plant species is a widespread adaptation for Fe mobilization from soil, mediated by the co-option of ancient microbial processes.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), an aggressive cancer with a poor prognosis, contains resident tissue macrophages (RTMs) present before tumor onset and monocyte-derived macrophages recruited during tumor development, but their distinct roles in supporting tumor progression remain unclear. Combining single-cell profiling, spatial analysis, lineage tracing, RTM depletion, and selenium tracing, we found that RTMs preferentially localize at the tumor border, where they promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), tumor growth, and metastasis. Mechanistically, RTMs transfer the selenium transporter Selenop to EMT

title: Switching of transcriptional control from interferon regulatory factor 2 to interferon regulatory factor 1 drives innate immune cell activation.
abstract: Interferon regulatory factor 2 (IRF2) is a transcription factor that prevents skin inflammation in mice and humans but, paradoxically, promotes pyroptosis by upregulating gasdermin D. How IRF2 activates some proinflammatory genes but suppresses inflammation is unclear. We show that skin inflammation in Irf2-deficient mice is driven by IRF1 activation of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Chromatin profiling reveals that IRF1 and IRF2 occupy the same ISG regulatory sites, but as a weaker transcriptional activator, IRF2 limits ISG transcription by IRF1. Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling favors IRF1-driven transcription by inducing Irf1. In addition, IRF1 recruits the ubiquitin ligase SPOP to ISG sites, resulting in proteasomal degradation of IRF2. This shift from IRF2 to IRF1 occupancy enhances ISG transcription. Collectively, these findings define a hierarchical transcriptional circuit in which IRF2 limits IRF1 activity under homeostatic conditions but is displaced during an immune response, allowing IRF1-dependent gene programs central to innate immunity and autoinflammation.

title: Toward autonomous science with agentic artificial intelligence.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in biomedicine has evolved from pattern-recognition for medical image analysis to generative models like AlphaFold that predict protein structures. Tools such as Elicit, GPT-Rosalind, and Claude Science now bridge prediction and reasoning through literature synthesis, domain-tuned models, and agentic workbenches. Three recent systems (Co-Scientist, Robin, and Biomni) demonstrated agentic AI capable of generating hypotheses, designing experiments, computational analysis, and refining reasoning through experimental feedback. This perspective traces the emergence of agentic scientific reasoning, discusses scaling laws and autonomous laboratories, and argues that AI's transformative potential is inseparable from challenges in hallucination, bias, irreproducibility, and dual use. Scientific progress will depend on responsible human-AI collaboration.

title: Ratiometric transcriptional activation by protein degradation.
abstract: Cells can respond to alterations in the abundances of specific proteins through transcriptional outputs. Synthetic approaches inspired by native post-transcriptional circuits that convert protein abundance changes into programmable gene expression would be transformative. Here, we discover and describe design principles that effectively convert protein degradation into transcriptional outputs in live cells. We define ratiometric transcriptional activation, where control over the ratio between a transcription factor and a protein of interest fused to its inhibitor enables detection of abundance changes with high sensitivity at scale. We show that ratiometric transcriptional activation can be implemented in single cells using triply orthogonal circuits or in multicellular pools, operating independently of the mechanism of protein downregulation and enabling simultaneous detection of multiple protein downregulation events through outputs such as cell survival, fluorescent protein expression, or barcode sequencing. These circuits can be applied to oncogenic targets and enable discovery of new molecular glue degraders.

title: Human nuclear ribomes reveal DNA-embedded ribonucleotides as epigenetic modulators of transcription-associated DNA supercoiling.
abstract: Ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) are the most abundant non-canonical nucleotides in DNA, yet their distribution and function in the human nuclear genome remain unclear. We present high-resolution maps of ∼1 million rNMPs per genome across diverse human cells, revealing a non-random nuclear "ribome," the genome-wide landscape of embedded rNMPs, enriched in GC-rich regions, regulatory elements, and telomeres. Ribonucleotide-enriched zones (REZs) cluster near transcription start sites (TSSs), coincide with C-phosphate-G (CpG) islands, R-loops, and G4 structures, and scale with gene expression. Ribonuclease (RNase) H2 deficiency increases rGMP levels and is associated with topoisomerase 1 (Top1)-dependent, strand-biased rNMP enrichment near TSSs, while Top1 depletion further enhances rGMP accumulation. RNase H2-mediated nicking at rNMPs alters DNA supercoiling in vitro, and RNH2A-deficient cells show altered supercoiling at rNMP-enriched TSSs. Our findings identify embedded rNMPs as epigenetic modulators of DNA supercoiling linked to DNA sequence and transcription, revealing a connection between ribonucleotide processing and transcription-associated DNA topology in human cells.

title: Ancient genomes reveal distinct human dispersals and social stratification in the settlement history of western Remote Oceania.
abstract: The settlement of western Remote Oceania involved interactions among deeply divergent populations. Initial settlement ∼3,000 years ago by Lapita-associated, Southeast Asian-related groups was followed by Papuan-related expansions and later sea voyages from Polynesia. We present genome-wide data spanning the past three millennia from the eastern Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Tonga. We find that the Papuan-related expansion proceeded at a slower pace than the earlier Lapita-associated expansion and reached Fiji through at least two distinct human dispersals, centuries earlier than previously suggested. We provide direct evidence of Polynesian-related gene flow at around 1,000 years ago, giving rise to Polynesian Outlier communities in southern Vanuatu. Finally, we examine an early Fijian community, revealing social practices that preserved wealth/status within a biological kin group with elevated Southeast Asian-related ancestry. Our findings refine the settlement model of western Remote Oceania and highlight the complex interplay of past migrations and community structure.

title: Metabolic atlas of early human cortex reveals glycolytic remodeling and pentose phosphate pathway control of cell fate transitions.
abstract: Cortical development involves rapid progenitor expansion and cell diversification supported by tightly regulated metabolic programs, yet these programs remain largely uncharacterized in human development. Here, we generated a metabolic atlas of the early human cortex using primary tissue and stem cell-derived cortical organoids. We observed dynamic changes in core metabolic functions, including an unexpected increase in glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) activity during late neurogenesis. Manipulation of glucose availability in cortical organoids altered cell-type composition, increasing outer radial glia (oRG) and inhibitory neuron populations. Pharmacological and genetic inhibition of PPP enzymes recapitulated these cell fate changes. Ribose was sufficient to rescue radial glia (RG) gene expression changes, revert organoid cell-type composition, and restore levels of ATP and hypotaurine. These data identify a critical role for the PPP in modulating RG cell fate specification and generate a resource for future exploration of additional metabolic pathways in human cortical development.

title: Milk osteopontin alters the infant microbiome to drive DC hematopoiesis and disease tolerance.
abstract: Breastfeeding reduces the risk of severe lower respiratory infections (sLRIs), a leading cause of infant mortality; however, the protective mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we demonstrated that the absence of milk-derived osteopontin (OPN), highly expressed in colostrum, predisposes neonatal mice to viral and bacterial sLRI, consequent to disrupted dendritic cell (DC) hematopoiesis in the developing liver and lung. Amelioration of disease severity by oral OPN supplementation was associated with increased enteric abundance of Lactobacillaceae and elevated levels of serum 3-phenyllactic acid (PLA), a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) agonist. Supplementation with PLA or the PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone restored lung DC hematopoiesis via airway epithelium-derived chemokine ligand 25 (CCL25)-mediated recruitment of lymphoid-myeloid primed progenitors and induction of a supportive lung niche. PLA-induced DC hematopoiesis and disease tolerance were attenuated by plasmacytoid DC depletion, immunoneutralization of stem cell factor, or genetic deletion of airway epithelial Flt3L. Our findings elucidate a microbiome-host interaction by which milk OPN confers protection against sLRI.

title: CRISPR screens identify targets to rescue age-related T cell dysfunction in cancer.

Abscisic acid (ABA) signaling is central to drought response, but its deep conservation can constrain adaptive flexibility. Here, we identify ROAD1 (rice orphan gene adapted for drought 1), an Oryza-specific orphan gene that confers robust drought tolerance without obvious growth defects under normal conditions. Endothelial AHR-APLNR signaling preserves vascular glycocalyx integrity and limits neutrophil-driven skin injury during local MRSA infection.
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major cause of skin and soft tissue infection, yet the contribution of the cutaneous vasculature to host defense remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify endothelial aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling as a key regulator of vascular integrity and inflammatory responses during local MRSA skin infection. MRSA challenge reduced AHR expression in cutaneous endothelial cells in both human and murine skin. Endothelial-specific AHR deficiency exacerbated skin injury, increased bacterial burden, enhanced inflammatory cytokine production, and promoted neutrophil accumulation and activation. Mechanistically, AHR-deficient endothelial cells induced exaggerated neutrophil calcium signaling and prolonged neutrophil-endothelial interactions during transendothelial migration. Loss of endothelial AHR was further associated with glycocalyx thinning, widened endothelial junctions, and vascular leakage, indicating impaired vascular barrier function. Pharmacological AHR activation partially reversed these abnormalities. Transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed that endothelial AHR maintained apelin receptor (APLNR) expression, whereas pharmacological inhibition of APLNR reproduced several inflammatory and vascular features observed in AHR-deficient mice. Collectively, these findings identify an endothelial AHR-APLNR-glycocalyx pathway that preserves vascular barrier integrity and restrains maladaptive neutrophil activation during MRSA skin infection, highlighting a potential therapeutic target for bacterial skin disease.

title: A pseudoenzyme sensor of trehalose-6-phosphate directly represses the metabolic integrator SnRK1 in plants.
abstract: Trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) is a central metabolic signal linking sugar availability to plant growth, carbon utilization, and productivity, yet its sensing and signaling mechanisms remain elusive. Using chemical biology and functional approaches, we identify the noncatalytic pseudoenzyme Class-II T6P synthase (TPS-II) as a T6P sensor in Arabidopsis. In the apo state, TPS-II dimerizes to form an autoinhibitory inter-subunit interaction. T6P binding to the N-terminal TPS-like domain triggers a conformational change that releases the C-terminal domain, enabling interaction with the central metabolic integrator SNF1-related protein kinase 1 (SnRK1) to repress its kinase activity. Loss of TPS-II genes activates catabolic and stress-responsive programs while suppressing anabolic gene expression, consistent with constitutive SnRK1 activity. Conservation of this T6P-TPS-II-SnRK1 signaling axis throughout the plant kingdom highlights its fundamental role in coupling carbon availability to metabolic homeostasis. These findings resolve a long-standing question in sugar signaling and provide a framework for improving crop carbon-use efficiency.
